items.title: Mat Domber interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007
items.q: we put Norman together with Warren Vache you know, and they play together beautifully.

ctx.x: Right. Again when I look at those lineups and even from the jazz parties that are still around, I see a lack of black musicians most of the time, or too often the time. Does that go back to what you were talking about before, they just don’t seem to fit into that?

We’ve always had black musicians or at least we’ve tried to have black musicians at our parties. We, again, I felt that the music is color blind and gender blind. We have women who we think are good performers who fit in. The whole issue is fitting in. I mean you know, Milt Hinton was at our parties while he was alive of course, and came — we honored him on his birthday as one of our — we had Benny Waters and we had Benny’s, I think he was 95 at the time, and we presented a tribute to Benny as part of our March…

to where the white musicians are playing, which is a shame because in the early days of music, the early days of jazz, although the country was segregated, the music wasn’t. And very often in the recording studios you’d have white and black musicians who were recording together while they couldn’t appear together on stage. And they jammed together and they learned from each other, and that was very, very interesting. Plus the fact that so many of the black musicians had teachers who were white. Buster Bailey, for…
